o: Order all passes chronologically; a streak is a maximal run of consecutive passes where passer and receiver share a team, and it belongs to that team. Any interception ends the current streak. For each team report its longest such run (0 if it never completed a pass). The classic SQL technique is the gaps-and-islands pattern: within each team, group consecutive successful passes by rn − row_number_in_group, then take MAX(COUNT(*)).
k: Gaps-and-islands: subtract each row's global chronological rank from its rank within (team, success-flag) partitions; equal differences identify consecutive runs.
Only successful passes (passer and receiver on the same team) participate; a failed pass breaks islands automatically because it is excluded and shifts ranks.
Teams with no successful passes must still appear with longest_streak 0 — handle via LEFT JOIN from Teams.

a.i: Rank passes chronologically, tag success, and use the rank difference trick to island consecutive successful passes per team; count island sizes and take the max per team.
s: CTE p: join both team names, compute ok = (teams equal), and rn = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY time_stamp).
CTE g: filter ok = 1 and compute grp = rn − ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY rn).
LEFT JOIN from Teams and take COALESCE(MAX(cnt), 0), ordered by team_name.

c.python:
-- MySQL 8+ solution
WITH p AS (
    SELECT tf.team_name AS tn,
           (tf.team_name = tt.team_name) AS ok,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY p2.time_stamp) AS rn
    FROM Passes p2
    JOIN Teams tf ON p2.pass_from = tf.player_id
    JOIN Teams tt ON p2.pass_to = tt.player_id
),
g AS (
    SELECT tn, rn - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY tn ORDER BY rn) AS grp
    FROM p WHERE ok = 1
),
c AS (
    SELECT tn, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM g GROUP BY tn, grp
)
SELECT t.team_name, COALESCE(MAX(c.cnt), 0) AS longest_streak
FROM Teams t
LEFT JOIN c ON c.tn = t.team_name
GROUP BY t.team_name
ORDER BY t.team_name;

a.i: Without window functions, walk passes in chronological order carrying the previous pass's team and success flag through user variables, incrementing a running streak and resetting on interception or team change; track the max per team in a temp aggregate.
s: Number passes chronologically with @rn via an ordered select into a derived table.
Using variables @prev_team/@prev_ok, compute streak = CASE WHEN same team AND previous ok THEN streak+1 ELSE 1 END for successful passes.
Group by team taking MAX(streak); LEFT JOIN from Teams for the 0 default.

c.python:
-- MySQL solution
SELECT t.team_name,
       COALESCE(MAX(s.streak), 0) AS longest_streak
FROM Teams t
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT tn, streak
    FROM (
        SELECT tn,
               @st := IF(ok = 1 AND tn = @pt, @st + 1, IF(ok = 1, 1, 0)) AS streak,
               @pt := tn
        FROM (
            SELECT tf.team_name AS tn,
                   (tf.team_name = tt.team_name) AS ok
            FROM Passes p
            JOIN Teams tf ON p.pass_from = tf.player_id
            JOIN Teams tt ON p.pass_to = tt.player_id
            ORDER BY p.time_stamp
        ) x, (SELECT @st := 0, @pt := '') v
    ) y
) s ON s.tn = t.team_name
GROUP BY t.team_name
ORDER BY t.team_name;

w: Prefer the window-function version — user variables are deprecated and rely on evaluation-order assumptions. The subtle point to articulate: why rn − partition_rank identifies consecutive runs (interceptions create rank gaps). Pitfalls: forgetting the LEFT JOIN for teams with zero successful passes, and assuming time_stamp format allows numeric comparison. Follow-up: longest streak ignoring halftime, or streaks of at least L passes.
